name: Amira Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Amira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the site lead for Kestrel Modular. We build houses in a factory, in big boxes, and then I take the crew out and we crane them onto the foundations and join them up. A whole house in a day, sometimes, then two weeks of finishing. This month we're doing twelve family homes in a village called Ashby Green. I'm up at five-thirty, I check the lorry schedule and the weather on my phone, and I'm on site by seven making sure the crane, the boxes and the crew all turn up at the same time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you keep all that in your head?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I don't, I use AI every day. It reads the weather, the lorry tracker and the crane booking and tells me where the clash is, and it writes my daily report while I drive. My husband Gábor runs his own electrical business, three vans, and I set him up with the same kind of tools for his quotes. Honestly, I'd be lost without it now, and I was the one who used to laugh at people who said that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it's a good tool and I'll keep using it. People who were afraid can calm down, and people like me will just keep being a bit quicker. I'd probably say it at the Sunday lunch with the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit sad. I'd been hoping it would get good enough that I could start my own modular firm one day with a small team. If it stays as it is, that dream takes longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Finish Ashby Green, keep using the tools, maybe help Gábor's business grow a bit. Keep paying the mortgage and saving towards that firm of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little bit flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much have you saved toward your own firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not as much as I'd like. We've got about four months of living money, and we've been putting fifty a month in a separate pot since Lili was born. It's more of a dream than a plan right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your crew would be glad if AI turned out to be hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stefan, my crane man. He's sixty and he calls my phone 'the boss'. He'd say, see, the boss was never in charge. And he'd be half right.

S0.say: It's a good tool and I'll keep using it, so the frightened people can calm down. I'd say it at Sunday lunch with the family.
S0.think: I'd be a bit sad, because I hoped it would get good enough for me to start my own modular firm with a small team. If it stays as it is, that dream takes longer.
S0.do: Finishes the twelve Ashby Green homes and keeps using AI tools daily. Helps her husband's electrical business grow and keeps saving towards a firm of her own.
S0.quote: He's sixty and he calls my phone 'the boss'.
S0.fieldNote: Amira is disappointed by a plateau because she sees AI as the route to her own business. She relies on it daily and already helps her husband use it. Her savings are modest and her own-firm idea is more dream than plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is an opportunity for people who work hard and pay attention. It's not a reason to panic, and it's not something the government needs to fix. I'd say that at work and to my brother, who'd disagree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well. Modular is already halfway to a factory, so it's ready for more machines. The question is whether I stay at Kestrel or start my own firm sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push Kestrel to bring in robots for the joining and finishing on site, and volunteer to lead the trial. I'd spend some of the savings pot on courses in robotic site equipment. And I'd talk to Gábor about whether his business and mine could join up one day, electrics and modular homes together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and honestly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your brother would disagree. What would he say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say the government should protect workers from this. I'd say the best protection is skills. We'd argue over the soup and then he'd ask me to help with his phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stefan, definitely, and maybe Joe, who's young but doesn't like screens. I'd tell Joe to learn now, while it's easy. Stefan's close enough to retirement that he can probably see it out.

S1.say: This is an opportunity for people who work hard and pay attention. It's no reason to panic, and it's not something the government needs to fix.
S1.think: I think I'd do well, because modular building is already halfway to a factory and ready for more machines. The question is whether I stay at Kestrel or start my own firm sooner.
S1.do: Pushes Kestrel to bring in robots for on-site joining and finishing and volunteers to lead the trial. Spends part of the savings pot on courses in robotic site equipment and talks with her husband about combining their businesses.
S1.quote: I'd say the best protection is skills.
S1.fieldNote: Her free-market outlook comes through as faith in skills over government protection. She sees modular building as naturally suited to more machines. She thinks practically about each crew member's chances.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is big, and people need to get ready fast. I'd tell everyone to learn the new tools and help each other, family first. I'd say it calmly, because panicking doesn't help anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, two years scares me. Even if I'm good with the tools, Kestrel could replace my whole crew, maybe me too. Gábor's business could go at the same time, if robots do wiring. We've got four months saved and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sit down with Gábor and look at the numbers. We'd stop putting money in the firm pot and build up living money instead. I'd push to become the person at Kestrel who sets up and runs the robots. And I'd ask Gábor to think about moving his business into installing and servicing robots, since that's electrics too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But it's the kind where I can still move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lili would ask, are we okay? I'd tell her, we'll work hard and we'll pray, and we'll be okay. Bence would ask if he can have a robot, and I'd say, you can help me fix one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said family first. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents have a bit of land and an old house. If it got bad, we could go there for a while. But I'd rather work. I'd sell my car before I'd ask for help.

S2.say: This is big and people need to get ready fast: learn the new tools and help each other, family first. I'd say it calmly, because panicking helps nobody.
S2.think: Two years scares me, because Kestrel could replace my whole crew, maybe me too, and my husband's business could go at the same time. We have four months saved and a mortgage.
S2.do: Stops saving for her own firm and builds living money instead. Pushes to run Kestrel's robots and urges her husband to move his electrical business into installing and servicing robots.
S2.feel: Anxious, but still able to move.
S2.quote: We'll work hard and we'll pray, and we'll be okay.
S2.fieldNote: Two years shakes her confidence because both household incomes are exposed. Her answer is to move towards the machines, not away from them. Faith and family appear as her safety net, but she'd rather work than ask for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty of time for anyone who wants to work. Learn the new skills, and businesses will need people who understand both the old way and the new. I'd say it to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough time for me to build something. I think I could start a small modular firm with Gábor, using machines from the start. It's risky, but I'd rather own the robots than be replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Kestrel for two years and learn everything about the robots there. We'd save hard, maybe three hundred a month. Then in year three, I'd leave and start the firm with Gábor, small, two or three people plus machines. We'd use the house as security for a loan if we had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than afraid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Using the house as security is a big risk. How would Gábor feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be nervous, he's the careful one. But he started his own business eight years ago with one van and a lot of prayer, so he knows what it takes. We'd agree on a line we won't cross, and stick to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that line be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm hasn't covered its own costs in eighteen months, we close it and go back to working for someone. We're not gambling the children's home on pride.

S3.say: Five years is plenty of time for anyone who wants to work. Businesses will need people who understand both the old way and the new.
S3.think: Five years is enough for me to build something: a small modular firm with my husband, using machines from the start. It's risky, but I'd rather own the robots than be replaced by them.
S3.do: Stays at Kestrel for two years to learn its robots while saving about 300 a month. In year three, leaves to start a small modular firm with her husband, possibly using the house as security for a loan with a firm 18-month cut-off.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but more excited than afraid.
S3.quote: We're not gambling the children's home on pride.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets her turn the threat into a business plan. She is comfortable with risk but sets a clear limit, which shows her family values. Her husband's past start-up experience gives them both confidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing. Use it to learn, build and look after your family. I'd say it at church and to anyone at work who's worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years means I can do this properly. I'd have time to save, learn and build the firm slowly. I'd be fifty-three, running something with Gábor, and the kids would be nearly grown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the robots at Kestrel first, then start the firm around year four or five with proper savings behind it. We'd buy machines as they get cheaper. I'd keep teaching the kids that hard work and skills matter, whatever the machines do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Lili and Bence to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lili loves drawing houses, so maybe design. Bence is always taking things apart. I'd tell both of them, learn to work with the machines and learn to work with people, and you'll always have a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd lose in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The crew, maybe. I like my crew, Stefan with his jokes, Joe with his music. A firm full of machines would be quieter. I'd want to keep a few people, even if I didn't strictly need them.

S4.say: Ten years is a blessing, so use it to learn, build and look after your family. I'd say it at church and to anyone at work who's worried.
S4.think: Ten years means I can do this properly, saving, learning and building the firm slowly. I'd be fifty-three, running something with my husband, with the kids nearly grown.
S4.do: Learns the robots at Kestrel, then starts her own firm around year four or five with proper savings behind it. Buys machines as they get cheaper and teaches her children to work with both machines and people.
S4.quote: A firm full of machines would be quieter.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Amira sees a clear path to the business she has long wanted. Her plan is patient and well funded rather than rushed. She'd keep people on even if she didn't need them, out of loyalty to her crew.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Gábor and I would both be hit and there'd be no time to build anything. What would help is cheap loans for small firms to buy machines, and fewer rules that make starting a business so slow.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. A lot of how I'd get through any of this is church and family. People forget that when they talk about the economy, but it's what holds us together when work doesn't.

headlineQuote: I'd rather own the robots than be replaced by them.
portrait: Amira Varga is a 43-year-old site lead for a modular house builder, married to an electrician with his own small business, with two children and about four months saved. She uses AI every day to juggle lorries, cranes and reports, and has long dreamed of starting her own modular firm. She's calm under a plateau and steady change, seeing skills rather than government as the best protection. Two years makes her anxious because both household incomes are exposed, but with five or ten years she'd learn the robots, then start a firm with her husband, owning the machines rather than being replaced by them.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and her husband would both be hit with no time to build anything.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans for small firms to buy machines, and fewer rules slowing down starting a business.
